The error burst and the restart eight seconds later are the pairing worth pursuing: either the CheckAvailability failures preceded a crash, or a restart (eviction, OOM, deploy) was already underway and the in-flight requests failed as it happened. Frontend logs alone cannot distinguish these. Next steps: pull the pod's termination reason and prior-container exit code, and query the search and reservation services across 21:09–21:11. Note the result is flagged truncated, so absence of errors near 21:17:39 should be confirmed with a narrower error-only query before being treated as settled.

found.statement: The only error-level lines frontend emitted in the queried 30-minute window are nine identical SearchHandler CheckAvailability failures, all stamped at a single second, 21:10:03 — roughly seven minutes before the 21:17:39 time of interest, not around it.

Eight seconds after that error burst, at 21:10:11, the frontend emitted a complete cold-start sequence (config read, Jaeger agent init, Consul agent init, gRPC client initialization, then serving HTTP), indicating the pod restarted immediately following the error cluster.

On restart the frontend successfully established gRPC connections to all five downstream dependencies it initializes (search, profile, recommendation, user, reservation) and reached the serving state without further error output.

The failing call path is the frontend's outbound availability check on the search handler, so the error is a symptom of a downstream dependency response rather than an internal frontend fault; the log line itself carries no status code or peer address to identify which dependency.
No error or exception lines appear at or near 21:17:39 in the returned data; the window ends at 21:17:45 with the last returned events being the 21:10:11 startup lines.

ruled_out.why: The returned lines contain no error entries after 21:10:03, and the post-restart output through the end of the window is informational only. Confidence is tempered because the result is marked truncated, so a later burst cannot be excluded with certainty.
ruled_out.hypothesis: The frontend was actively emitting errors at 21:17:39, the time the investigation anchored on.

ruled_out.why: All nine error lines share one timestamp second; the preceding 22 minutes of the window produced no error lines at all. This is a point burst, not a sustained condition.
ruled_out.hypothesis: The frontend errors were a sustained, continuous failure spanning the half-hour window.

ruled_out.why: Exactly one startup sequence appears in the window, at 21:10:11, and it runs to completion ending in the serving state. A loop would produce repeated init sequences.
ruled_out.hypothesis: The frontend is stuck in a crash loop, restarting repeatedly.

ruled_out.why: The restart sequence shows Consul agent initialization succeeding and gRPC connections being obtained for every one of the five downstream services, with no connection errors logged.
ruled_out.hypothesis: The frontend failed to reach or resolve its downstream services, or had a broken Consul/service-discovery or gRPC client configuration.

ruled_out.why: The startup lines show config read, log level, GC tuning, and TLS state all emitted at info level with no accompanying error, and the process proceeded to serve traffic.
ruled_out.hypothesis: A TLS, logging, or startup configuration problem caused the frontend failure.

ruled_out.why: No panic, stack trace, or fatal-level line appears; the only pre-restart output is a handled application-level error from the search handler.
ruled_out.hypothesis: The frontend crashed on an unhandled panic or exception.

verdict.reasoning: The only substantive change in the window is a CPU ceiling cut on the frontend itself; no image, version or flag change exists [tr_ec5e968a606a]. The restart timestamp matches the edit to the second and shows healthy service discovery and five successful downstream connections [tr_44133780e673], which argues against a wrong address, credential or dependency as the mechanism. The post-restart signature is absence rather than failure: flat-zero error ratio with zero variance plus intervals containing no spans at all [tr_a1e1555af34a, tr_d2052c256486] and silent logs [tr_44133780e673] — work not completing while nothing errors is what throttling looks like from outside the container. The downstream story is weak: the nine CheckAvailability failures are a single-second burst at 21:10:03, before the alert, and never recur [tr_44133780e673], while reservation logged no CheckAvailability activity at all [tr_eacfd29a4cab]. Traces could have arbitrated but returned nothing for frontend across the whole window including the healthy period, so the trace path is itself impaired [tr_adf228881c31]. The fix is restoring the previous CPU limit.
verdict.root_cause: Platform automation halved the frontend workload's CPU ceiling (limits.cpu 1 -> 500m, request raised to match) about seven minutes before onset [tr_ec5e968a606a]. The edit recreated the pod: a full cold-start sequence appears at 21:10:11, one second after the change, with all five downstream gRPC clients connecting cleanly [tr_44133780e673]. From that point the frontend goes quiet — no further log output [tr_44133780e673], zero error spans across 22 samples [tr_a1e1555af34a, tr_d2052c256486], and three intervals with no spans at all, meaning it served nothing in those intervals [tr_a1e1555af34a, tr_d2052c256486]. That is CPU starvation under the new ceiling: requests stall rather than fail, so callers hang while the frontend reports no errors. The limit edit is how it started; exhaustion is the failing mechanism.

alternatives.why_not: It does not explain the alert at 21:17:39, and a concrete CPU-limit cut landing seven minutes before onset is a better fit than instrument failure [tr_ec5e968a606a].
alternatives.root_cause: The frontend telemetry pipeline is broken and the apparent outage is an observability gap rather than a service fault.

alternatives.why_not: The only evidence is a single-second error burst before onset that never recurs [tr_44133780e673]; no trace or metric data identifies a slow downstream, and reservation's logs are empty [tr_eacfd29a4cab, tr_adf228881c31].
alternatives.root_cause: A downstream dependency behind the search/availability path became slow, and the frontend hung waiting on it.

open_questions: No container-level data was ever returned — CPU throttling ratio, restart counts and OOM/eviction events were requested but absent [tr_d2052c256486]; throttling is inferred, not measured.

Why frontend traces are missing for the entire window including the pre-incident baseline, and why a zero-result query was flagged truncated [tr_adf228881c31] — a broken telemetry pipeline would undermine the 'no spans means no traffic' inference.
What the 21:10:03 CheckAvailability burst actually hit; the log line carries no peer or status code and reservation's logs are empty under that filter [tr_44133780e673, tr_eacfd29a4cab].

draft.title: Frontend goes silent after a CPU ceiling edit

sections.body: The page came from the frontend, and the declared blast radius was six services with critical severity. Five of the edges between frontend and its downstream neighbours had no measurement on them at all, which shaped everything that followed: for most of the investigation we were reasoning about a service whose own telemetry was thin and whose dependency links were unobserved. Anchor time (T+0) is the moment of interest the page carried; everything below is written as an offset from it.
sections.heading: What the page said and where we started

sections.body:
The obvious first move was to read the frontend's own output across the half hour leading up to T+0. The only error-level lines in the entire window were nine identical availability-check failures from the search handler, all stamped within a single second at roughly T-7m36s. Eight seconds later a complete cold-start sequence appears: config read, tracing agent init, service-discovery agent init, gRPC client setup, and then the serving state. All five downstream gRPC clients connected cleanly. After that the log is quiet — nothing at or near T+0, no panic, no stack trace, no second startup sequence.

This ruled out several comfortable stories in one pass. It was not a crash loop (one startup, run to completion). It was not a service-discovery or client-config problem (every downstream connection succeeded). It was not a TLS or startup-config problem (all those lines are informational). And the errors were not sustained — they are one point burst, not a condition spanning the window. The caveat worth carrying forward: the log result came back flagged truncated, so a later burst cannot be excluded with full certainty.
sections.heading: First pass: frontend logs

sections.body:
The natural follow-up was the span-derived error ratio for frontend. It is flat zero — twenty-two samples, mean, min, max and standard deviation all exactly zero — over both the narrow and the widened window. No error creep, no spike, nothing. Whatever was wrong, it was not reaching users or callers as errored frontend spans, and no downstream failure was propagating into frontend as error status.

Two things made this more than a null result. First, three intervals returned no defined value at all. For a ratio of this shape that means no spans whatsoever in those intervals, which is a traffic gap and not a healthy zero — frontend stopped serving at points in the window. Second, the comparison baseline window produced no samples, so there is no before/after delta. The tooling's own 'no sustained departure' verdict rests on an empty baseline and should not be read as reassurance.

We also asked this same path for container-level signal — throttling ratio, restart counts, eviction or out-of-memory events. None of it came back. The only series returned was the error ratio. That gap is still open.
sections.heading: Dead end: the frontend error ratio

sections.body:
With logs quiet and the error ratio flat, traces were the obvious way to find a terminal error span and rank the downstream callers by latency. The query returned nothing for frontend across the full thirty minutes — not just the failing minute, but the pre-incident stretch too. So there was no span tree, no blame attribution, and no healthy baseline to compare against.

Two plans died here: naming the culprit dependency from span status codes, and identifying a dominant latency contributor by comparing child durations. Both need spans that do not exist in the store. One oddity is worth recording: the empty response was also flagged truncated, which is strange for a zero-result query and weakly hints at something wrong in the trace query path rather than a clean absence of data. That matters, because the 'three intervals with no spans means no traffic' inference above leans on the trace pipeline being honest.
sections.heading: Dead end: traces

sections.body:
The point burst at T-7m36s was an outbound availability check, so the handler name was the one concrete thread we had. Searching the reservation pods for that handler across the same window returned nothing at all — not errors, not ordinary request logs. That is a weaker result than it looks: zero matching lines is equally consistent with reservation genuinely being quiet and with reservation simply not logging under that wording, or logging at a level that suppresses request lines, or not shipping logs from those pods.

So this did not clear reservation, and it did not implicate it. It only closed the log path. Any case for or against reservation has to come from somewhere else.
sections.heading: Dead end: reservation's side of the failing call

sections.body:
The change record was the thing that moved us. Three entries exist for frontend in the window, all from the same platform automation actor, none human-initiated. The frontend workload and its Service object were created roughly nine minutes before T+0, meaning this instance was newly stood up immediately before the incident rather than long-running. Then, about seven minutes before T+0, a resource-limits edit landed: the CPU ceiling was cut in half and the CPU request was raised to equal the new ceiling.

That edit lines up exactly with what the logs show. The cold start at roughly T-7m28s is one second after the change — the edit recreated the pod. The error burst eight seconds prior is the old instance on its way out.

The change record also closed doors. There is no image or application version change, so a code deploy is out. There is no flag toggle in the window. And 'nothing changed on frontend, this must be environmental' is directly contradicted by three recorded entries, one of which is a CPU ceiling reduction.
sections.heading: What actually turned the investigation

sections.body: Platform automation halved the frontend's CPU ceiling about seven minutes before onset; the edit recreated the pod, which came up clean and connected to all five downstream services. From that point frontend produces no further log output, zero error spans across twenty-two samples, and three intervals with no spans at all. That shape — silent, error-free, intermittently serving nothing — is what CPU starvation under a tightened ceiling looks like. Requests stall rather than fail, so callers hang while the service itself reports nothing wrong. The limit edit is how it started; starvation under that limit is the failing mechanism. Confidence is medium, and the fix class is reverting the config.
sections.heading: Conclusion

sections.body:
Three things were never resolved and would change the strength of the conclusion.

No container-level data was ever returned. Throttling ratio, restart counts, and out-of-memory or eviction events were all asked for and all absent. The throttling is inferred from the change plus the silence, not measured. Getting that series is the single highest-value next step.

Frontend traces are missing for the whole window including the pre-incident baseline, and a zero-result query came back marked truncated. If the trace pipeline is itself broken, then 'no spans means no traffic' is unsound and the traffic-gap finding needs re-deriving from another source.

What the burst at T-7m36s actually hit is unknown. The log line carries no peer address and no status code, and reservation's logs are empty under that filter. A broader filter, a different selector, or non-log telemetry would be needed to settle it.
sections.heading: Still open for the next responder

proposal.risk: If the diagnosis is wrong this is a wasted recreate of the alerted user-facing service, dropping in-flight requests and its in-process cache. Restoring a 1-core ceiling also lets frontend push more load downstream; if the real fault is a saturated dependency, this deepens it. It also reverses a platform-automation action, which may be re-applied and flap unless that automation is paused.
proposal.if_wrong: Falsified if, 10 minutes after the revert and its cold start, frontend span rate is still undefined/zero and Loki still shows nothing past the startup block. Note two live doubts: container-level throttling, restart and OOM data were never returned [tr_d2052c256486], so starvation is inferred not measured; and Tempo returned nothing for the whole window with a truncated flag [tr_adf228881c31], so if logs show traffic while span metrics stay empty, suspect the telemetry pipeline rather than a failed fix.
proposal.blast_radius: frontend is recreated: external callers see resets for the restart duration. Its five downstream dependencies (profile, recommendation, reservation, search, user) see traffic stop, then resume at possibly higher volume.
proposal.expected_effect: Restoring frontend's prior resource config (limits.cpu 1 / requests.cpu 100m, undoing the 500m/500m edit at 21:10:10 [tr_ec5e968a606a]) and recreating the container should let frontend complete requests again. Observable as: the frontend span rate denominator becoming defined and non-zero in every 5m interval (no repeat of the three no-span intervals), and the frontend Loki stream emitting request lines beyond a single cold-start block instead of going silent as it did after 21:10:11.
